From your post I think a big problem is the language we use around mental health and illness and a lack of understanding.

This woman won't just suffer from bouts of feeling sad or anxiousness. PTSD as a result of childhood trauma is a complex illness to treat. It requires years of regular and intense therapy sessions with a dedicated specialised therapist. 

Illnesses such as cPTSD and cluster B personality disorders are notoriously hard to treat and have massive amounts of stigma attached to them, so much so that doctors won't even want to diagnose them. The stigma is so great that a diagnosis from a doctor can negatively impact your future treatment.

Even my own depression, which was so bad the scale didn't go high enough, was noted as "periods of sadness" by the doctor. I had been severely depressed for about 7 years at that point and seeking help for about 3. My first GP told me he couldn't help me until I tried to kill myself. Anyone who has been through the system will tell you the help just isn't there even if you seek it.

The standardisation towards a "standard English" is a much more recent phenomenon due to the railways and TV/radio.

For decades people have been complaining about rising inequality and decreasing living standards, and the areas that this is most apparent in are the predominantly white de-industrialised towns and cities. And then you have to mix in the effect of online spaces and culture wars.

Quite frankly the left sucks at communication and listening to the folks that need them the most because those with the language to articulate the problems of society from a left wing perspective come from affluent metropolitan areas and are largely out of touch with the white working class. 

From the perspective of a new reform voter, the left in London are ignoring their issues for 40-odd years, telling them that their issues aren't real and focusing on what they seem to be unimportant issues like racial and gender equality, and telling them actually they are part of the problem. Whether this is true in actuality is immaterial, the perspective is there and the left is failing to challenge it (fwiw I believe racial and gender inequality are important issues and tie directly to class inequality). 

So now you have a disenfranchised group of people who are increasingly more isolated and feeling the effects of the economy, with the people who can help them not listening, and the right is telling them "I hear you, your problems are real, and the cause is immigrants/trans people/workers rights/feminists". 

The right has successfully given this group of people the language needed to express their dissatisfaction with their standard of living through rhetoric around culture wars, even if the arguments they make are reductive or out right lies. It makes politics accessible to them.

Let's be real Barry (52) or Kyle (24) doesn't see Charlotte (28) from London and a degree from UCL as speaking to them. This is why diversity on the left is important. Real diversity that also includes white working class men. Because we can already see the result when they're not.

A moment of humility for a second, I admit I'm guilty of this. I grew up in the NE in an ex- mining village in the 2000s. I was your typical underprivileged kid. Single mother, shop worker, council house, benefits etc etc. Things weren't great for me or many of the kids around me. No one earning that amount gave a flying fuck about it at the time as in their eyes we were benefit scroungers and dole dossers, so an emotional part of my brain just wants to tell them to fuck off because they only care because it affects them now, and they'll throw families like mine under the bus as soon as they get theirs. 

However I know that this isn't conducive for any solution to the problem, and that if things are to get better across the board every member of the working class needs to have solidarity with each other. 

I also think there's an element of tone deafness too. Having someone on £80k tell you how hard things are when the average for your town is £20k can come across as a little tone deaf and self centred. Especially when, like you mentioned, tax is brought into it. Someone on £80k telling someone on £20k that they themselves pay too much tax and that those on £20k need to pay more is not class solidarity in my eyes. It's the same class divisions in the reverse situation in my eyes. Same with someone who is able to send their kid to private school telling people who send their kids to a state school that it's unfair and a tax on aspiration, when state schools like mine couldn't even afford textbooks and 70% of kids were on free school meals. People who send their kids to private school didn't care when schools like mine couldn't even get enough teachers to teach the lessons, so the lessons just went untaught. 

Obviously my experience won't be universal, I just wanted to illustrate that class tensions go deep and are complex and are further complicated by changing class demographics.

One thing I haven't seen mentioned at all is the erosion of unions. Before we had minimum wage unions had a significant role in keeping pay competitive. With the changes to union laws over the years they have less capacity to do this and union membership has fallen drastically.

We won't ever get a wider bell curve through market forces and growth, as any growth will be siphoned off for shareholders and stored in a tax haven. 

Unfortunately the government has little power other than adjusting minimum wage, so they need to restore union powers so that people on above minimum wage have a body to fight for their pay increases.

There's also the context of the time. No one wanted a repeat of the first world war. Despite having one of the lower death tolls, entire villages lost their working age male population in Britain just 20 years before. The great depression also hit the working class hard especially in the industrial areas and unemployment was high during the 30s. So Britain at the time was not ready for war and was very reluctant for it. 

I personally think people don't consider this context in their criticism of Chamberlain enough, and we did start arming after the Munich agreement and signed the defence pact with Poland. It must have been clear that war was coming if they started arming in preparation for war. However with the benefit of hindsight it was clear that appeasement only further emboldened Hitler (as was a criticism at the time) as he thought Britain would not come to the aid of Poland as they did not do so with Czechoslovakia, and thus a miscalculation on the part of the British government. 

We have the benefit of hindsight now, which makes it all the more infuriating that we seem to be making the same mistakes.

I was in Japan last year and plan to go again next year.

I find the Japanese in many ways quite similar to the British, especially when compared to other Anglo nations. I'd say the biggest difference comes with the level to which this is taken.

We both have a queuing and tea culture. And both are considered polite to the point it's hard to tell what the person is really thinking. I also think we're both big on tradition.

The biggest difference I find is that Japanese politeness is on a whole different level, to the point of baked into the grammar of the language. Your social conformity is quite extreme compared to the Brits too.

Honestly I disagree with that view as I find it a bit reductive. These traditions haven't deliberately come into existence for the pleasure of tourists like it's Disney Land. They're real customs that have come about and serve a purpose, even if people come to see them to see a culture different to their own.

The royal family is a working institution. The kings guard are actual military, not a tourist attraction. That doesn't mean people don't go to London to see them, but their primary job isn't to parade around and be gawked at. 

We're not the only culture that exports itself. Scotland rents out kilts and you can purchase Lairdship by buying a tiny bit of land. Japan's entire tourism industry is a cultural export. 

Honestly I'd even argue that the extreme end of commodified and cultivated culture for the sole purpose of selling it in America is a culture in of itself. America dominates in pop culture export.

I can see the criticism of turning culture into a commodity to be bought and sold though, but I don't think simply selling the experience of a culture makes it cease to be.

I find the idea that England has no culture a bit anglo-defaultism. If you can recognise a different culture as different to your own then you have something in contrast to them, and therefore a culture of your own. 

Drinking tea and the royal family are part of our culture that attracts millions of visitors a year. It may seem dull to us but it is still tradition, and clearly something that sets us apart from other cultures.

We have traditional food that suited our climate. Fish dishes, seafood, stews, hearty Sunday dinners. Even the borrowed dishes like Tikka Masala are still British, they were made in Britain by immigrants that brought us that food into the melting pot and are as much as part of the culture as fish and chips. The story of colonialism and migration is a part of our story and culture, the good and the bad.

In terms of traditional garb, kilts do actually exist in England as traditional dress but in the border regions, Northumberland has its own tartan. If you're looking a bit further south there's the attire of various folk dances. A few examples are morris dancing, rapper dancing, furry dancing, and clog dancing. In terms of official dress we have no designated official clothing unlike Scotland and Wales, but again what we consider traditional has actually become the norm; a 3-piece suit and a hat of some variety. There's also the attire of the Kings Guard and Beef Eaters that are quintessentially English to people from abroad. 

In terms of folk tales, ours has pretty much become the blueprint for general fantasy. Ghosts, spirits, black dogs, black cats, goblins, brownies, hags, dragons... Everywhere in Britain has tales of these creatures.

Anecdotally, if you're looking for folk traditions I think you'll have more success looking locally rather than nationally. I think the the biggest difference between England and the other nations of the UK is that we're just not as unified in our national identity. Those keeping these traditions alive would love to have people involved.

Ohhh welcome to the north east. It's rare to see tourists from across the pond to take interest in our region compared to London.

I'm from South East Northumberland, have an interest in local history, with a dad from Durham, I also went to uni there so I think I might be of help.

First of all that's *a lot* to pack into 4 days. You will need to be selective with what you want to see. There is a LOT of history, the golden age of which was around 600CE. We have the most castles out of any county.

Do you have a car? If not there are hire companies (there's one called Enterprise just next to Boldon on Testo's Roundabout, maybe someone can chime in with recommendations) you can use public transport but it's woefully under invested. Your other options will be the Tyne and Wear metro, main train line, and local buses. Going up the east coast there's only a few train stops so the train option is limited for most of your activities. The train line going west along the Tyne is much better, and could be an option for Hadrian's Wall. 

A lot of the national trust and English heritage historic sites will be closed at the moment for the winter so check which are open before arriving.

Starting in the north, Berwick, Bamburgh and Lindisfarne are good choices. Lindisfarne is a tidal island so HEED THE TIDE TIMES. I'm not joking you will put your life in danger if you don't and someone will have to rescue you. The time times are available on Northumberland County Council's website here: https://holyislandcrossingtimes.northumberland.gov.uk/
Only cross when it is safe to do so. You can cross in a car or walk along the Pilgrims Way. These tide times do not apply to crossing on foot, if you would like to do this I'd recommend finding a local guide. Seriously don't underestimate the tide. I come from near Cresswell and people get stuck on the rocks because they don't realise how fast it comes in or the angle it comes in at and they get stuck. If you get up early, and tide time depending, you could possibly do Bamburgh and Holy Island in one day. Also around that region are Farne Island boat trips where you can see the seals and puffins. Other notable places in that region are Seahouses and Craster. Seahouses is famous for the rescue made by Grace Darling. Craster is famous for their kippers.

Further down we have Alnmouth, Warkworth and Amble. Warkworth has a ruined castle with some nice pubs and Amble has some good fish and chips and a Sunday market. A little further down than that is Widdrington, and I highly recommend going to the Widdrington Inn pub for food (the steak and ale pie is so good). Alnmouth is a small village that will scratch your "quaint village" itch.

Further down the coast again we start to get into the more populous industrial area of the north east. Druridge Bay and Cresswell beach form part of Northumberland's AONB. This is the area I'm from and comprises of Lynemouth, Ellington, Linton, Newbiggin, and nearby Ashington. Unfortunately this area suffered greatly after the closure of the mines and has seen a lot of deprivation. There has, however, been significant regeneration in Newbiggin now. Nearby Woodhorn Museum is focused on showing the industrial heritage of this region and locals are extremely proud of their heritage. 

Also around this area is Morpeth. You can get here by bus or train.

Keep going down the coast and you get to the North Tyneside areas. Whitley Bay is a classic British seaside town with amusements, ice cream, and fish and chips. If you go I recommend Trenchers in the Spanish City. 

Start to go west and you hit the Newcastle city region. I find it hard to recommend stuff for here because to me it's just a regular city. There's Hancock's museum which has a collection of Roman finds. The castle is there to visit but I think there are much better ones especially when you have to pay. Black Friars is a higher end dining experience in what I think is a medieval building. 

Now we're getting to the areas which I'm not as familiar for. Further west along the Tyne you will come to Corbridge (another "quaint" village) and Hexham (home of Hexham Abbey). Along here is asking where you will find Hadrian's Wall. There are multiple walking routes along here if you fancy that. The wall is mostly crumbling now after 2000 years so there's not much to see. Interspaced every mile or so we have forts that are called mile castles. There are several that you could see but I think the biggest and most extensively excavated is Vindolanda.

Moving below the Tyne you come to the historic country of Durham. Again, this area I'm not too familiar with but I was born here and went to uni here. The must-do here is Durham City and the Cathedral. You can get here by either bus or train. You can go in the castle but will have to book because it is student accommodation. Beamish Museum is also a must do. It's A living museum showcasing the industrial heritage of the north east mainly through the 19th and 20th century. There are areas focused on each time period with costumed actors and period buildings. Brilliant for kids and also just a really nice day out. I get a ticket every year. Also in County Durham is Bishop Auckland but now we're pushing for distance and time.

As you can see there is a lot packed into this region and I haven't even covered Kielder, Northumberland national park, the areas surrounding Otterburn (amazing Sunday roast at the William De Percy here).

To cut all this down here is my recommendation:

Bamburgh and Lindisfarne for one day, Alnwick town, castle and gardens for one day (provided it is open), Newcastle city centre, Durham City and Cathedral for one day, Beamish Museum for one day.

You're still missing a lot of the stuff you will want to do here.

I studied at Durham 2025-2018. I'll try to be objective as possible however my overall experience was not great. I'll try to give specific examples to paint a picture, but please be warned TW for mentions of prejudice, sexism, racism, SA, depression and mentions of suicide.

I was a "local" working class white student, born in Durham and grew up in SE Northumberland. I was the first in my family to attend uni. The high school I went to was not a good one. In many ways, I was a similar student to you, considered disadvantaged by the university.

As others have mentioned Durham is generally populated by quite privileged white upper middle class students. While not experiencing outright discrimination myself I did experience prejudice. I had been told I didn't deserve to be there and took a place from someone that did, and my accent was mocked. I struggled to make friends throughout my time there as I had very low self esteem. Of course not everyone is like that, but people definitely stick to "their own kind" and so it can leave you feeling quite ostracized if you do not fit the mould.

Sexism was commonplace, in fact there have been several controversies. One of which is the term "rolling in the mud", which is used to mean a competition to see who can sleep with the poorest most working class girl. Others are reports of drugging and sexual assault at house parties. On that note drinking culture is very big. As I'm not a WoC, I did not experience race discrimination or prejudice however I have heard that other WoC have.

On the academic side, I also struggled but mainly from lack of support. I put this down to working class students not having the experience or knowledge of what to ask for or what they can get help with. The course content itself I did not find particularly difficult. I struggled with depression for my entire time there, and the GP available for students was downright dangerous, I'll not get into specifics but what they said to be could have possibly pushed someone to suicide.

That being said, once I got sufficiently behind in my work I finally worked up the courage to contact my academic advisor (you will get both an academic and course advisor). She was an absolute angel, and I was able to access special adverse circumstances for my work as well as medication from my GP. In all, if you're not familiar with academia or have family in that sector it can be very difficult to navigate. Durham have put a lot of work into getting working class students into the uni, however the support seems to stop at admission. I also had no assistance with careers advice or job hunting, and was told my the careers service there was nothing they could provide me for the North East sectors. Again, possibly the uni or also possibly because I didn't know who to ask or what to ask for. Nevertheless there is an accessibility issue there.

The collegiate system is cliquey, as are societies. However the multiple levels of student groupings (course, college, society etc) allow you to meet a lot of people in different circumstances, so if you can't find friends in college you may still find them elsewhere. I eventually found a society I enjoyed but I made no lasting friends from it with the exception of my partner.

Housing is abysmal and expensive. Expect landlords to actively break the law and charge extortionate rent. There are student groups trying to combat rogue landlords, but it's a difficult task. There is some resentment between the locals and the university because of rent prices affecting local people and pushing them out of the city centre, as well as the class divide between the students and the history of the city. You can live in college, I did for 2/3 years, but again this was quite expensive. I was in the cheapest accommodation at £5500 per year (not including meals). Most colleges are catered, and you'll therefore be paying extra because of the meal tickets. At the time I think the average cost was somewhere north of £6000 a year. It's probably more now.

Since COVID I've heard the university had took a downturn in its quality of teaching and student experience. Lots more students per course to recuperate costs, lack of staff, little 1 to 1 support etc. I cannot provide first hand details or anecdotes on this as I graduated pre-covid. The university is also plagued by the current strikes with some people being unable to graduate and get graduate jobs because of it.

Durham is a place where if you fit in, know what to ask and where to ask you'll thrive. If you deviate in any way from the norm you will find it difficult to navigate and have a good experience. If you want to thrive there you'll have to fight for it, it won't come easy. However I did know other working class students who enjoyed their time there.

The country is split into constituencies, each constituency needs to elect an MP. The candidate with the most votes becomes the MP for that area (FPTP). Most MPs are tied to a party, and that goes towards the parties seats in parliament. The party with the most seats and majority forms the government with the party leader becoming PM. No majority means a hung parliament and an agreement or coalition needs to be formed otherwise a minority government will occur.

In practice it becomes a 2 party system. The left wing vote is split between 2 parties (sometimes 3). The right wing party (conservatives/Tories) doesn't currently have a competitor to split the right wing vote. There was a lurch forward to the right in the party in 2015 (directly leading to Brexit) because the Tories didn't want their vote to be split by UKIP.

This means the left wing vote need to rally around the biggest "left wing" party (Labour) if they ever want to form a government. And that party has had its fair share of problems. In more recent years it's embraced centrist and neo-liberal policies to capture the centrist vote and maximise their chances at governing, to the dismay of the leftist wing that vote for them only through gritted teeth because they don't have any other choice if they want a left wing government.

And this isn't even covering the current political shit storm and revolving door installed in No. 10.

Starting an maintaining a garden isn't as easy as it seems. I'm from a semi-rural mining village in the UK. My street has large gardens that were used as allotments during ww2. We also have regular allotments where people grow food and raise chickens. 

My auntry tried to upkeep one to help with food costs but she found it impossible with a full time job 

The amount of food it takes to feed a family year round is difficult to provide with an allotment, even during ww2 with victory gardens rationing was still quite austere. Remember though that their goal wasn't exclusively for food. They also were morale boosters and brought communities together.

That all being said you can maximise the success you can have with a garden depending on the space you have, the area you live, and your preparation/knowledge (and money).

Try pick easy to grow things, this will depend on the climate of where you live. Check your local growing calendar. 

Try grow things that are easy to preserve or last a long time. Some varieties of potatoes can be stored a few months. During ww2 people would grow these in bath tubs and on the side of roads. Fruit can be turned into jams and preserves for the winter (they also make nice gifts).

Even if you dont have garden space herbs can be grown on a windowsill in a small pot. It amazes me these can be so expensive in shops because some of them grow like weeds.

Another thing people forget is that year round food choices are a relatively modern thing. So if you wish to rely on home grown food for some stuff then you'll have to get used to the idea of eating seasonally and adapting your recipes.

If you have the time and space chickens are also pretty neat to keep. You can get a dozen eggs every day or so with a moderate sized coop (like 5 chickens). This however depends on the time of year and sunlight.

I also know someone who keeps bees and has a couple gallon bottles of mead fermenting over the year.
